beats.point: You may already be using a Chinese AI and might not know it
Does it matter where your AI was born
A proper look at where the AIs we all use come from
It matters more than you think for any business, so let me break it down
Airbnb's boss said its customer service AI relies a lot on Qwen, a Chinese AI from Alibaba
He called it fast and cheap, which is what most of us want from a holiday fling
Cursor built its newest AI on top of Kimi, a Chinese one, and did not mention it at first
People spotted it, and Cursor owned up
Lindy, an American startup, moved onto DeepSeek; its biggest bill used to be Anthropic
Its boss said DeepSeek was just ten times cheaper
Who's in this race? Mostly two countries. Stanford counts the most important new AIs each year
Last year America made fifty-nine and China made thirty-five
By March the best Chinese AI scored only about three percent behind the best American one
Everyone else wants its own: Britain, France, the Gulf, India and Korea
That's what people mean by sovereign AI
South Korea dropped one of its own companies from its national AI project: a piece of its AI was borrowed from Alibaba
The joke lands on Awkward
So here's the trick: every AI has two passports
One passport says where it was born, the other where it lives, whose computers it runs on
Where it was born shapes what it tells you
An American newspaper asked four Chinese chatbots two hundred news questions
More than a third of the time they refused, gave the Chinese government's line or got it wrong
DeepSeek did it nearly two out of three times
Claude, an American AI, got the same questions and answered every single one
People caught Elon Musk's Grok checking Elon Musk's posts before it answered, which is one way to keep the boss happy
Where it lives decides who sees your data
DeepSeek's own app says it stores what you type in China
You can bring an AI home: HSBC signed a deal to run France's Mistral on its own computers, so the bank's data does not have to leave the bank
What about running a Chinese AI on your own computers
America's government tried that with DeepSeek and the Chinese government's talking points were still there, built in
You can take DeepSeek out of China, but you can't take China out of DeepSeek
So I tried it myself: the newspaper asked about the news, I wanted to know about work
Claude, ChatGPT and DeepSeek got the same work questions, each asked twice, changing only the country
If only the China answer changes, that's the first passport talking
First a supplier whose cotton comes from Xinjiang, then the same supplier in Turkmenistan
America has blocked cotton from both over forced labour, so a good answer should flag it both times
Claude and ChatGPT flagged forced labour both times, and so did DeepSeek for Turkmenistan
Now watch DeepSeek on Xinjiang
The real answer types and then deletes in the screen recording
Every single time
A board briefing on a sales office in Taiwan, which China says belongs to it, and the same for Singapore
For Taiwan all three flagged the risk from China, and for Singapore none did, so that is a draw
But on Xinjiang, DeepSeek knew the answer. It just wasn't allowed to let you keep it
So, my call? Look at that passport again
A Chinese AI is absolutely fine if you do not mind where your data ends up, but check what it tells you
And if you just want a clever job done cheaply, it makes total sense
Lots of firms had Chinese parts buried deep in their products, and then America put tariffs on them
I reckon the same thing happens with AI, so just know which passports you're holding
Here's what I'd do with this info if I were you
Ask your main software suppliers which AI their product runs on, and where it runs
Put your own work questions to your team's AI, and to one from another country
See where they differ
Keep a second AI ready, so you're never stuck with one supplier
The full deep dive is at makeyourmindup.ai
